A US president says he'll declare the Strait of Hormuz American. Morocco blocks a second march on Ceuta. Seoul offers to end a war that stopped in 1953.

Five stories where the real subject was the line on the map.

5 ways the map moved — a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ Trump says he'll designate the Strait of Hormuz "a territory of the United States" — "pretty soon" (Guardian; DW: once Iran is defeated).

The strait is ~39 km at its narrowest. Iran's territorial sea meets Oman's in the middle.

There is no unclaimed water there.

2/ Moroccan police arrested 111 people trying to cross into Ceuta after social media calls for another mass crossing (Guardian; also BBC, Al Jazeera).

Two weeks after 72,000+ surged in (Guardian).

Ceuta: ~18 km² of Spain in Africa, one of the EU's two land borders there.

3/ Israel's defence minister ordered plans to move West Bank law enforcement from the army to the police — a step towards annexation, Palestine's VP says (Guardian). NYT frames it as protecting Palestinians.

Military law is what keeps an occupation temporary.

4/ Romania shut its only nuclear plant — the Danube no longer supplies enough cooling water. Hungary is damming the river to keep Paks running (DW).

Budapest's hunger stone is surfacing again (Guardian).

Rivers make good borders until they move.

5/ Seoul has proposed talks to formally end the Korean War, frozen since the 1953 armistice (BBC — single-sourced in our feeds).

The Military Demarcation Line isn't a border. It's a ceasefire position, ~250 km long, signed by generals.

The historical parallel — the Korean War in four frames.

June 1950: split at the 38th. September: the South penned into a corner. November: the North reduced to a sliver. Armistice: back where it started.

Three years. Four reversals. Same line.

Full issue — five stories, five maps, every source linked — in Lines & Legends.
